newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Tietmeyer - EMU stability no threat to jobs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Tietmeyer - EMU stability no threat to jobs.

text.p: Europe's plans to create a stable currency union with lasting fiscal austerity do not contradict efforts to tackle stubbornly high jobless rates, the president of Germany's central bank said on Wednesday.

One day after Europe's political leaders met in Amsterdam to push European integration forward, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer welcomed summit decisions and said Europe would not pay for fiscal austerity with still higher jobless rates.
"There is absolutely no contradiction between the stability pact and the goal of conquering joblessness," Tietmeyer told a news briefing before accepting a prize from a state craftmen's association.
Calling the stability pact another step towards European integration, Tietmeyer said stable monetary and sound fiscal policies laid the foundation for healthy economic growth, including jobs growth.

He said he regretted the recent flurry of suggestions that Germany's high jobless rate could be blamed on the Bundesbank's strict stability oriented policy. He rejected talk that higher inflation rates could jump-start jobs creation.

"Inflation not only creates greater uncertainty for companies but also creates disadvantages for those who receive fixed incomes and those who save...(and it) harms economic efficiency," Tietmeyer said.

The existence of over four million jobless in Germany has long worried the Bundesbank but officials have repeatedly said interest rates were at sufficiently low levels to stimulate economic growth. The problem was rather caused by rigid labour structures and a host of other problems including tax laws seen by many as a disincentive to local investments.
"An increase in jobs cannot be expected from long-term higher inflation rates," Tietmeyer warned, adding "economic theory and experiences have proven this many times."

He said the solution did not lie with either state sponsored spending programmes or expansive monetary policies, nor could the unemployment problem be blamed on Europe's headlong rush towards currency union.
Tietmeyer argued existing problems could only be tackled through sound fiscal policies and that an unstable currency union with a weak curreny "would be a costly mortgage."
"Only a durable, successful currency union with a stable currency and without greater conflicts can move Europe forward," Tietmeyer said.
As the clock ticks toward the selection next spring of those nations to be among the first to join currency union, Tietmeyer steered clear of any comment about who might be in or out.
He also sought to defuse a simmering conflict on the exact meaning of the fiscal criteria by urging all to read the Maastricht Treaty.

"I can only suggest that one should read the Treaty where the reference values are spelled out and the conditions under which one could deviate from these are also spelled out," Tietmeyer said, adding that for him the key issue was sustainability for public finances.
He touched only briefly on the bitter row between the Bundesbank and the German government over Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plans to revalue gold reserves and use these to paper over fiscal holes.
Hinting that a resolution was in sight Tietmeyer said a meeting would take place this week and preliminary discussions had brought the two sides closer together.
"I expect that we will reach a final solution, including on the details, very soon," he said.

The Bundesbank has signalled to the Bonn government that it would be willing to revalue its currency reserves, now listed in the central bank's books at historic lows, and Tietmeyer said any decision would be compatible with the law.
